concepts.title: Microbe Diversity and Culturing on Nutritive Media
concepts.definition: Microorganisms span protozoa, bacteria, fungi, microscopic plant and animal viruses, viroids and prions, thriving everywhere from hundred-degree thermal vents to acidic pools and deep soil; bacteria and many fungi can be raised on nutritive media into visible colonies, which is what makes laboratory study of them possible.
concepts.key_idea: Only a handful of microbes cause disease -- the vast majority are neutral or useful, and their tiny size hides an enormous metabolic range.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 1-21 (microbe groups, extreme habitats, colony growth on media)
question_patterns: which groups of organisms count as microbes
what are prions and viroids
name the extreme habitats where microbes survive but other life cannot
how are bacteria and fungi grown in the laboratory for study
why can microbe colonies be seen with the naked eye
which kingdoms of living organisms contain micro organisms

solution_steps.explain: The microbial world includes protozoa, bacteria, fungi, viruses of plants and animals, viroids and the protein-only prions.
Microbes occupy soil, water, air and living bodies, and persist in geysers near 100 degrees, metres under snow, highly acidic sites and deep soil.
On nutritive media bacteria and many fungi multiply into colonies big enough to see, the working unit of microbiology studies.

concepts.title: Microbes in Household Products: Curd, Dough and Cheese
concepts.definition: Every kitchen runs on microbes: lactic acid bacteria such as lactobacillus turn milk into curd, their acids coagulating and partly digesting milk proteins while boosting vitamin b12 and checking pathogens in the stomach; bacterial fermentation puffs dosa and idli dough with carbon dioxide, baker's yeast raises bread, palm sap ferments into toddy, and propionibacterium sharmanii blows the holes into swiss cheese while a ripening fungus flavours roquefort.
concepts.key_idea: A spoonful of curd works as starter (inoculum) because millions of lab cells carry the fermentation forward -- the same logic behind every traditional fermented food.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 77-105 (curd/LAB, dosa-idli dough, bread, toddy, Swiss and Roquefort cheese)
question_patterns: how does milk get converted into curd and which bacteria do the work
why does curd improve the nutritional quality of milk
what makes dosa and idli dough puff up
which microbe ferments bread dough and which gas is released
why does swiss cheese have large holes in it
how do the bacteria in curd help inside the human stomach

solution_steps.explain: Lactobacillus and other lactic acid bacteria added as starter multiply at warm temperatures; the acids they make coagulate and partially break down milk proteins, and vitamin b12 levels rise.
Dosa and idli batter ferments through bacteria whose carbon dioxide inflates it; bread dough uses saccharomyces cerevisiae, baker's yeast.
Toddy comes from fermented palm sap, and fish, soyabean and bamboo shoots are fermented into traditional foods.
Each cheese's texture and taste traces to its microbe: propionibacterium sharmanii's carbon dioxide carves swiss cheese's holes, and a specific fungus ripens roquefort.

concepts.title: Fermented Beverages and Brewer's Yeast
concepts.definition: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the same brewer's yeast used in bread, ferments malted cereals and fruit juices into ethanol on an industrial scale inside large vessels called fermentors; wine and beer stop at fermentation, while whisky, brandy and rum take the extra step of distilling the fermented broth.
concepts.key_idea: One yeast, one reaction, two product families -- distillation is the only divide between wine-and-beer and whisky-brand-rum.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 106-134 (fermentors, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, distilled versus undistilled drinks)
question_patterns: which yeast is used in brewing and what does it produce
how do wine and beer differ from whisky brandy and rum in processing
what are fermentors and why does industry need them
which raw materials are fermented to make alcoholic drinks
recall the metabolic reactions behind ethanol production by yeast
why is saccharomyces cerevisiae called brewer's yeast

solution_steps.explain: Brewer's yeast, saccharomyces cerevisiae, does the fermenting in huge industrial tanks called fermentors.
Malted cereals or fruit juices supply sugars that yeast converts into ethanol, the reaction behind every alcoholic drink.
Wine and beer are served straight from the fermented broth; whisky, brandy and rum are distilled from it -- the raw material plus this step decides the drink.

concepts.title: Antibiotics: Penicillin and the War on Bacteria
concepts.definition: Antibiotics are chemicals some microbes make to kill or stall other microbes -- against microbial life but pro human life; penicillin surfaced by chance when fleming noticed a penicillium notatum mould wiping out staphylococci on an unwashed plate, chain and florey later proved its full power, and the trio shared the 1945 nobel prize as the drug went on to tame plague, diphtheria, whooping cough and leprosy.
concepts.key_idea: A forgotten dirty plate opened the antibiotic era -- and after penicillin, purified antibiotics from many other microbes followed.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 135-168 (antibiotic definition, Fleming's discovery, Chain and Florey, WWII use, diseases controlled)
question_patterns: define antibiotics and explain the meaning of the word
recount how alexander fleming discovered penicillin
which mould produces penicillin and what was it originally named after
what contribution did chain and florey make to the penicillin story
name the deadly diseases antibiotics brought under control
why were fleming chain and florey awarded the nobel prize in 1945

solution_steps.explain: Antibiotic joins the greek anti (against) with bio (life): these are microbial chemicals that kill or retard disease-causing microbes while helping human patients.
Fleming, studying staphylococci, saw a mould on an unwashed plate around which the bacteria could not grow; the mould's chemical was named penicillin after penicillium notatum.
Chain and florey unlocked penicillin's full clinical value, allied troops used it widely in world war ii, and the 1945 nobel prize crowned all three.
Antibiotics purified from further microbes turned plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy from mass killers into treatable diseases.

concepts.title: Industrial Chemicals, Enzymes and Bioactive Molecules
concepts.definition: Fermentor-grown microbes also supply organic acids (aspergillus niger for citric, acetobacter aceti for acetic, clostridium butylicum for butyric, lactobacillus for lactic), ethanol from yeast, working enzymes -- lipases for oily laundry stains, pectinases and proteases that clarify bottled juices, streptokinase as a clot buster after heart attacks -- and medicines such as cyclosporin a from trichoderma polysporum for transplant patients plus statins from monascus purpureus that competitively block cholesterol synthesis.
concepts.key_idea: Match the product to its maker -- each acid, enzyme and drug has one named microbe, and examiners love that pairing.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 169-190 (acid producers, lipases, pectinases, streptokinase, cyclosporin A, statins)
question_patterns: match each organic acid to the microbe that produces it industrially
which enzymes clarify bottled fruit juices
how do lipases help in detergent formulations
what is streptokinase used for and which bacterium yields it
name the microbe sources of cyclosporin a and statins
how do statins lower blood cholesterol in the body

solution_steps.explain: Citric acid comes from the fungus aspergillus niger; acetic acid from acetobacter aceti, butyric acid from clostridium butylicum, lactic acid from lactobacillus -- all bacteria.
Saccharomyces cerevisiae makes commercial ethanol; lipases strip oily stains in detergents, while pectinases and proteases give bottled juices their clarity.
Streptococcus-derived streptokinase, modified by genetic engineering, dissolves blood-vessel clots in patients after myocardial infarction.

Trichoderma polysporum yields cyclosporin a, the immunosuppressive that protects organ transplants; monascus purpureus yeast makes statins, which competitively inhibit the enzyme that synthesises cholesterol.

concepts.title: Sewage Treatment: Primary, Secondary Stages and BOD
concepts.definition: Municipal waste water, or sewage, is scrubbed in two stages at treatment plants: primary treatment removes particles physically by sequential filtration and sedimentation, giving primary sludge and an effluent; secondary treatment aerates that effluent so heterotrophic microbes in flocs eat the organic matter, cutting the biochemical oxygen demand until flocs settle as activated sludge, part of which recycles to the aeration tank while the rest feeds anaerobic digesters that release methane-rich biogas.
concepts.key_idea: Bod is the yardstick of pollution -- the oxygen microbes would need to oxidise a litre's organic load -- and treatment runs until that number drops enough for rivers to cope.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 191-271 (primary/secondary treatment, flocs, BOD, activated sludge, digesters, Ganga and Yamuna action plans)
question_patterns: differentiate primary from secondary sewage treatment
what is bod and why does it measure the polluting power of waste water
what are flocs and what role do they play in aeration tanks
what is activated sludge and why is part of it pumped back into the tank
which gases do anaerobic sludge digesters release and what are they worth
why can sewage not be released straight into rivers and streams

solution_steps.explain: Primary treatment is purely physical: floating debris goes through sequential filtration, grit settles out, solids collect as primary sludge and the supernatant effluent moves on.

In aeration tanks, agitated and air-pumped, useful aerobic microbes grow as flocs -- bacteria tangled with fungal filaments -- and consume most of the organic matter, sharply lowering the effluent's bod.
Once the bod falls, the flocs sediment in a settling tank as activated sludge; a little returns as inoculum for the aeration tank and the bulk goes to anaerobic sludge digesters.

solution_steps.action: Harvest the gas, release the water
solution_steps.explain: Anaerobic bacteria digest the sludge, emitting methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide -- an inflammable biogas mix -- while the treated effluent is safe enough for rivers; the ganga and yamuna action plans extend this capacity.

concepts.title: Biogas: Methanogens and the Gobar Gas Plant
concepts.definition: Methanogens -- anaerobic bacteria such as methanobacterium that grow on cellulosic material -- emit plentiful methane alongside carbon dioxide and hydrogen, making biogas; they flourish in sewage sludge and in the rumen of cattle where they help digest cellulose, so cattle dung (gobar) seeds the typical biogas plant: a 10-15 feet concrete tank of slurry under a floating cover whose pipe delivers cooking and lighting gas, with spent slurry out as fertiliser.
concepts.key_idea: The rumen connection explains everything -- the same cellulose-digesting methanogens that help cattle digest make gobar gas possible.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 272-324 (methanogens, rumen, gobar gas, plant design, IARI and KVIC)
question_patterns: which bacteria produce biogas and under what conditions
why are methanogens found in the rumen of cattle
describe the parts of a typical biogas plant
why is biogas commonly called gobar gas in india
what happens to the spent slurry from a biogas plant
which indian institutions developed biogas technology

solution_steps.explain: Methanogens such as methanobacterium grow without oxygen on cellulosic substrates and give off chiefly methane plus carbon dioxide and hydrogen; fermentation of dough or cheese by contrast yields mainly carbon dioxide.
In the rumen of cattle these bacteria break down cellulose, aiding the animal's nutrition -- hence dung, or gobar, teems with them and fuels gobar gas.

A concrete tank 10-15 feet deep holds the bio-waste and dung slurry; a floating cover rises as gas collects, an outlet pipes biogas to houses for cooking and lighting, and spent slurry exits as fertiliser.
Rural areas suit the plants best since cattle dung is abundant there, and iari together with kvic drove the technology's Indian development.

concepts.title: Biocontrol: Ladybirds, Bt, Trichoderma and Baculoviruses
concepts.definition: Biocontrol manages pests with living agents instead of toxic chemicals: ladybird beetles eat aphids and dragonflies hunt mosquitoes; bacillus thuringiensis spores sprayed on brassicas die inside caterpillar guts releasing their toxin; the free-living root fungus trichoderma fights several plant pathogens; and nucleopolyhedrovirus baculoviruses give species-specific, narrow-spectrum control that leaves beneficial insects unharmed -- ideal for organic farming and integrated pest management.
concepts.key_idea: Organic farming keeps pests at manageable levels through ecological checks and balances rather than eradicating them -- predators need prey to survive too.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 325-386 (organic farming logic, Ladybird, Dragonflies, Bt, Trichoderma, Nucleopolyhedrovirus, IPM)
question_patterns: what is biocontrol and why is it preferred over chemical pesticides
which insects are controlled by ladybirds and dragonflies
how does bacillus thuringiensis kill butterfly caterpillars
what is bt cotton and how was it created
why is trichoderma a useful biocontrol agent of plant pathogens
what makes nucleopolyhedrovirus ideal for integrated pest management

solution_steps.explain: Biodiversity keeps a landscape sustainable: pests are held down by a living web of predators and parasites, not exterminated with insecticides that poison soil, water, food and people.
The red-and-black ladybird beetle clears aphids; dragonflies pick off mosquitoes.

Dried bacillus thuringiensis spores mixed with water are sprayed on brassicas and fruit trees; larvae eating them get the toxin released in their guts and die, other insects stay safe -- and engineered bt toxin genes created bt-cotton.

Trichoderma species, free-living in root ecosystems, suppress several plant pathogens; nucleopolyhedrovirus baculoviruses attack only narrow insect targets with no harm to plants, mammals, birds, fish or beneficial insects -- perfect for ipm and ecologically sensitive areas.

concepts.title: Biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Mycorrhiza and Cyanobacteria
concepts.definition: Biofertilisers are organisms that enrich soil nutrients, easing the pollution burden of chemical fertilisers: rhizobium in legume root nodules and free-living azospirillum or azotobacter fix atmospheric nitrogen into usable organic forms; glomus mycorrhizal fungi absorb phosphorus for the plant and earn resistance to root pathogens plus salinity and drought tolerance in return; and cyanobacteria such as anabaena, nostoc and oscillatoria fix nitrogen in paddy fields while adding organic matter.
concepts.key_idea: Symbiosis does the fertilising -- bacteria trade nitrogen, fungi trade phosphorus, and both draw sugars from the plant partner.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo108.txt lines 387-421 (chemical fertiliser problems, Rhizobium nodules, Azospirillum/Azotobacter, Glomus mycorrhiza, cyanobacteria in paddy)
question_patterns: what are biofertilisers and why switch to them from chemical fertilisers
how does rhizobium in legume root nodules help the plant
name the free living nitrogen fixing bacteria of soil
what benefits do plants draw from glomus mycorrhizal associations
which cyanobacteria serve as biofertilisers in paddy fields
what does the fungus gain from a mycorrhizal partnership

solution_steps.explain: Rhizobium lives in nodules on legume roots, turning atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms the plant uses as nutrient.
Azospirillum and azotobacter do the same trick loose in the soil, raising its nitrogen content without any host.

Glomus members form mycorrhiza whose fungal partner absorbs phosphorus from soil and hands it to the plant, which gains root-pathogen resistance, salinity and drought tolerance and better growth -- while the fungus feeds on the association.
Autotrophic cyanobacteria -- anabaena, nostoc, oscillatoria -- fix nitrogen in paddy fields, add organic matter and lift soil fertility, cutting dependence on chemical inputs.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo108.txt lines 470-478 (exercise 11: assigning BOD values to water samples, reworded)
worked_examples.question_pattern: Three unlabeled water samples give bod readings of {sample_a}, {sample_b} and {sample_c} mg per litre. Decide which is most polluted and identify the river water, the untreated sewage and the secondary effluent.

solution_template.explain: Higher bod means more organic matter for microbes to oxidise, hence more pollution: 400 far exceeds 20 and 8.
Sample c (400 mg/l) is untreated sewage; sample a (20 mg/l) is the secondary effluent, cleaned but not pristine; sample b (8 mg/l) is the relatively clean river water.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo108.txt lines 181-190 and 494-497 (streptokinase, cyclosporin A, statins; exercise 12)
worked_examples.question_pattern: Name the microbial source of {drug_one} and of {drug_two}, and state what each is used for.

solution_template.explain: Cyclosporin a is produced by the fungus trichoderma polysporum and given to organ-transplant patients to suppress rejection.
Statins come from the yeast monascus purpureus and lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting its synthesising enzyme.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo108.txt lines 99-105 (Swiss cheese holes and Roquefort flavour)
worked_examples.question_pattern: Swiss cheese is full of large holes while roquefort owes its sharp taste to a mould. Explain which microbe causes each feature.

solution_template.action: Blame the gas for the holes
solution_template.explain: Propionibacterium sharmanii releases large amounts of carbon dioxide during fermentation, and the escaping gas carves swiss cheese's holes.

solution_template.action: Credit the mould for the flavour
solution_template.explain: Roquefort is ripened by growing a specific fungus on it, which supplies the characteristic flavour; cheese variety generally follows the microbe used.
